research.topic: arkit-mesh-depth: ARKit scene reconstruction (ARMeshAnchor), LiDAR scene depth, ARFrame/ARCamera, ARWorldMap, raycasting, session lifecycle on the iOS 18 runtime / iOS 26 SDK (LiDAR iPhone 13 Pro Max)

facts.claim: Scene reconstruction is enabled by setting `sceneReconstruction` on ARWorldTrackingConfiguration to `.mesh` or `.meshWithClassification`; both options and the property were introduced in iOS 13.4, nothing about them is deprecated on the iOS 26 SDK. Requires a LiDAR device; iPhone 13 Pro Max has LiDAR.
facts.notes: Doc: if plane detection is also enabled ARKit flattens the mesh where it detects a plane; if people occlusion frame semantics are enabled ARKit removes mesh overlapping people. Use `.meshWithClassification` for wall/floor/ceiling/door/window/table/seat labels (RealityKit's automatic session disables classification by default, so set `arView.automaticallyConfigureSession = false` and run your own config).

facts.claim: Check device support before enabling: `ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(_:)` (class func, iOS 13.4). Also `ARConfiguration.isSupported` (class var).
facts.api:
class func supportsSceneReconstruction(_ sceneReconstruction: ARConfiguration.SceneReconstruction) -> Bool
class var isSupported: Bool { get }
facts.notes: Returns true only on LiDAR devices.

facts.claim: Scene depth is requested via `frameSemantics` on the configuration with `.sceneDepth` and/or `.smoothedSceneDepth` (both iOS 14). Check with `supportsFrameSemantics(_:)` (class func). FrameSemantics is an OptionSet, so `config.frameSemantics = [.sceneDepth, .smoothedSceneDepth]` or `.insert(...)` both compile.
facts.notes: Apple point-cloud sample checks `ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsFrameSemantics([.sceneDepth, .smoothedSceneDepth])`. sceneDepth = discrete LiDAR reading for that frame; smoothedSceneDepth = temporally averaged (less flicker, more latency). Both can be enabled at once and both then populate on every ARFrame.

facts.claim: `ARFrame.sceneDepth` / `ARFrame.smoothedSceneDepth` are `ARDepthData?` (nil unless the semantic is enabled). `ARDepthData.depthMap` is a CVPixelBuffer of `kCVPixelFormatType_DepthFloat32` ('fdep'), one Float32 per pixel in METERS from the camera plane; `confidenceMap` is `CVPixelBuffer?` of `kCVPixelFormatType_OneComponent8` ('L008') holding ARConfidenceLevel raw values (low=0, medium=1, high=2). Resolution is 256 x 192 (landscape, same aspect ratio and field of view as capturedImage 1920x1440), delivered at 60 Hz with every frame.
facts.notes: Pixel formats are verified in Apple docs (depthMap doc names kCVPixelFormatType_DepthFloat32 -> MTLPixelFormat.r32Float; confidenceMap doc names kCVPixelFormatType_OneComponent8 -> .r8Uint/.r8Unorm). The 256x192 figure is not in the doc text but is hard-coded in Apple's own 'Displaying a point cloud using scene depth' sample (`origDepthWidth = 256, origDepthHeight = 192, origColorWidth = 1920, origColorHeight = 1440`) and confirmed by multiple third parties (openMVS issue 1055: cv::Mat(192,256,CV_32F)). Always read actual size with CVPixelBufferGetWidth/Height instead of hard-coding. WWDC20 10611: depth is RGB+LiDAR fusion via ML, 60 Hz, a value on every ARFrame. Max useful LiDAR range about 5 m, min about 0.5 m (Apple DTS, forum 130326); the fog sample comments 'The LiDAR Scanner supports a value no larger than 5.0'.

facts.claim: To unproject a depth pixel you must scale `camera.intrinsics` (which is in full camera-image pixels) by depthWidth/imageWidth and depthHeight/imageHeight. Apple's sample does exactly: `cameraIntrinsics[0][0] /= scaleRes.x; cameraIntrinsics[1][1] /= scaleRes.y; cameraIntrinsics[2][0] /= scaleRes.x; cameraIntrinsics[2][1] /= scaleRes.y` with `scaleRes = cameraResolution / depthResolution`, then `x = (u - cx) * depth / fx; y = (v - cy) * depth / fy; z = depth` in camera space (note ARKit camera space is +x right, +y up, -z forward; the sample's z = depth is a 'camera looks down +z' convention, so negate z and flip y before applying camera.transform to get ARKit world coordinates).
facts.api:
var intrinsics: simd_float3x3 { get }   // column-major: intrinsics[0][0]=fx, [1][1]=fy, [2][0]=ox, [2][1]=oy (pixels)
var imageResolution: CGSize { get }
facts.notes: Intrinsics doc: 'fx, fy pixel focal length; ox, oy principal point offset from top-left of the image; all in pixels'. Intrinsics describe capturedImage in native (landscape) sensor orientation. Depth/confidence buffers share that orientation and normalized (0..1) coordinates with capturedImage, so sampling depth at the same normalized texcoord as the color image is correct (both Apple samples do this).

facts.claim: `ARFrame.capturedImage` is a CVPixelBuffer in full-range bi-planar YCbCr 4:2:0 (kCVPixelFormatType_420YpCbCr8BiPlanarFullRange, '420f'): plane 0 = Y (8-bit, use MTLPixelFormat.r8Unorm), plane 1 = interleaved CbCr (half res, .rg8Unorm). It is in the camera's native sensor orientation (landscape-right), so a portrait UI must rotate it; the doc gives the YCbCr->RGB matrix (ITU-T T.871). Default resolution on iPhone 13 Pro is 1920x1440 @ 60 fps.
facts.notes: Doc verifies 'full-range planar YCbCr ... ITU R.601-4'; the exact constant name comes from Apple's Metal AR template and every Metal sample (texture creation with .r8Unorm plane 0 / .rg8Unorm plane 1 verified in Apple's point cloud sample). For a photo/texture pipeline convert with vImage/CoreImage (`CIImage(cvPixelBuffer:)`) or a Metal compute kernel. Do not retain ARFrames (WWDC22 warns retention causes frame drops and tracking to go 'limited').

facts.claim: ARCamera per-frame pose and projection accessors. `transform` is camera-to-world (right-handed; camera space +x along long device axis, +y up, +z toward the user, i.e. camera looks down -z). `projectionMatrix` (property) equals projectionMatrix(for:) with imageResolution, landscape orientation, zNear 0.001, zFar 1000.
facts.notes: World space: gravity-aligned (+y up) with `worldAlignment = .gravity` (default); `.gravityAndHeading` aligns -z to true north (needs location); `.camera` uses initial camera pose.

facts.claim: On the iOS 26 SDK the orientation-based ARCamera/ARFrame helpers still exist under their Swift names `projectionMatrix(for:viewportSize:zNear:zFar:)`, `viewMatrix(for:)`, `projectPoint(_:orientation:viewportSize:)`, `unprojectPoint(_:ontoPlane:orientation:viewportSize:)` and `ARFrame.displayTransform(for:viewportSize:)`. Apple's current doc set marks them deprecated at iOS 27.0 (not 26) in favour of new `viewRotationAngle:` variants that are iOS 27-only, so for an iOS 18 deployment target you must use the orientation variants (they compile; at worst a warning on a 27 SDK).
facts.availability: orientation variants iOS 11.0+ (unprojectPoint iOS 12.0+), listed as deprecated 27.0 in Apple's doc JSON; viewRotationAngle variants iOS 27.0+
facts.notes: Swift spelling of the orientation variants verified in compiled open-source code (introlab/rtabmap RTABMap.swift: `frame.camera.viewMatrix(for: orientation)` and `frame.camera.projectionMatrix(for: orientation, viewportSize: viewport, zNear: 0.5, zFar: 50.0)`; satoshi0212/AR_100Days: `frame.displayTransform(for: .landscapeRight, viewportSize:)`) and Apple's own ObjC pages (projectionMatrixForOrientation:viewportSize:zNear:zFar:, viewMatrixForOrientation:, displayTransformForOrientation:viewportSize:) which the JSON marks 'deprecated 27.0'. If zFar == 0 an infinite projection matrix is returned. The projection is aspect-FILL for the viewport.

facts.claim: ARMeshAnchor exposes one `ARMeshGeometry` chunk; ARKit subdivides the reconstructed scene into many mesh anchors and keeps updating them (not real-time). Chunks are roughly 1 m x 1 m 'square' patches (community measurement), triangle density is higher on surfaces scanned up close.
facts.notes: Chunk size (~1 m squares, some overlapping) is community evidence only (saboit.de blog, medium 'ARKit 911'); Apple publishes no numbers for chunk extent, vertex spacing or update rate. Practical planning figure (unsure): a furnished room yields tens of anchors and on the order of 10^5 triangles total. ARMeshAnchor does NOT conform to ARTrackable. Mesh anchors are identified by `identifier` (stable across updates); treat didUpdate as 'replace this chunk's geometry'.

facts.claim: ARMeshGeometry accessors: `vertices` and `normals` are ARGeometrySource with format `.float3`, componentsPerVector 3, count = vertex count (normals count == vertices count, one per vertex despite doc prose saying per face); `faces` is ARGeometryElement with primitiveType `.triangle`, indexCountPerPrimitive 3, bytesPerIndex 4 (UInt32), count = triangle count; `classification` is an optional ARGeometrySource with format `.uchar` (1 byte per FACE, count = face count, raw ARMeshClassification, 0 = .none). Buffers are MTLBuffer with `.storageModeShared` (CPU and GPU readable). Vertex positions are in the anchor's LOCAL coordinate space; multiply by `anchor.transform` for world space.
facts.notes: Apple's own extension code (from the docs): vertex(at:) = `vertices.buffer.contents().advanced(by: vertices.offset + vertices.stride * Int(index)).assumingMemoryBound(to: SIMD3<Float>.self).pointee` (assert format == .float3; stride may include padding so never assume 12); face indices = `faces.buffer.contents().advanced(by: (faceIndex * indexCountPerPrimitive + k) * MemoryLayout<UInt32>.size)` read as UInt32; classification = `classification.buffer.contents().advanced(by: faceIndex).assumingMemoryBound(to: UInt8.self).pointee`. Anchor-local space confirmed by Apple DTS (forum 682585) and the subscript doc ('offset relative to its parent anchor's position'). ARMeshClassification raw values in declaration order: none=0, wall=1, floor=2, ceiling=3, table=4, seat=5, window=6, door=7 (order taken from the ObjC header; doc topic lists alphabetically). SceneKit bridge: `SCNGeometrySource(buffer:vertexFormat:semantic:vertexCount:dataOffset:dataStride:)` + `SCNGeometryElement(data:primitiveType:primitiveCount:bytesPerIndex:)`; copy the buffers, the ARMeshGeometry buffers are reused/reallocated on update.

facts.claim: Mesh anchors arrive through the normal anchor delegate callbacks on ARSessionDelegate: `session(_:didAdd:)`, `session(_:didUpdate:)` (the [ARAnchor] overload), `session(_:didRemove:)`; filter with `anchors.compactMap { $0 as? ARMeshAnchor }`. Frames arrive via `session(_:didUpdate frame: ARFrame)`. `ARFrame.anchors` also lists all current anchors. Delegate callbacks run on the main queue unless `session.delegateQueue` is set.
facts.notes: Set `delegateQueue` to a serial background queue to keep mesh copying off the main thread; the geometry buffers are only valid until the next update for that anchor, so copy vertex/index data inside the callback. Apple's sample processes faces on `DispatchQueue.global()`. A forum report (iPad Pro 4th gen, iOS 18 era) describes mesh anchors being removed and re-added after 5-30 s; handle didRemove gracefully and keep your own persistent copy keyed by identifier.

facts.claim: ARMeshAnchors are NOT included in an ARWorldMap (Apple DTS engineer, forum 705469). ARWorldMap contains only non-ARTrackable anchors present at capture (custom ARAnchors and ARPlaneAnchors are persisted; ARMeshAnchor is excluded by the framework). Persist the mesh yourself (your own serialized vertex/index/classification arrays per anchor, in world space) and optionally add a plain ARAnchor per chunk to the map for relocalization.
facts.notes: Doc wording ('all anchors whose positions are assumed static, i.e. classes that don't conform to ARTrackable') would suggest inclusion, but the DTS answer and the practical experience of everyone who tried say mesh anchors are dropped; the ARAnchor doc adds that anchor subclasses must implement NSSecureCoding to be saved, which ARMeshAnchor's geometry is not. Save timing: check `frame.worldMappingStatus` is `.mapped` or `.extending`. On resume, tracking starts `.limited(.relocalizing)` and becomes `.normal` when the map is matched; if the place differs it stays limited forever, so give the user a 'start fresh' escape.

facts.claim: ARWorldMap serialization: `NSKeyedArchiver.archivedData(withRootObject:requiringSecureCoding: true)` and `NSKeyedUnarchiver.unarchivedObject(ofClass: ARWorldMap.self, from:)`; load by setting `configuration.initialWorldMap` and running with `[.resetTracking, .removeExistingAnchors]`.
facts.notes: Apple sample 'Saving and loading world data' (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/saving-and-loading-world-data). Map size scales with scanned area and feature count; typically single-digit to tens of MB for a room (unsure, community). `rawFeaturePoints.points: [simd_float3]` can be used to judge map quality. Calling getCurrentWorldMap on a non-world-tracking configuration fails immediately with an error.

facts.claim: ARFrame.worldMappingStatus reports map quality: `.notAvailable`, `.limited`, `.extending`, `.mapped`. Camera tracking state: `.notAvailable`, `.limited(ARCamera.TrackingState.Reason)`, `.normal` with reasons `.initializing`, `.relocalizing`, `.excessiveMotion`, `.insufficientFeatures`. Tracking changes are also delivered via `session(_:cameraDidChangeTrackingState:)`.
facts.notes: Use these to drive scan UI ('move slower', 'more light') and to gate world-map saving.

facts.claim: Light estimation: `isLightEstimationEnabled` (default true) fills `frame.lightEstimate` with `ambientIntensity` (lumens-ish, 1000 = neutral) and `ambientColorTemperature` (Kelvin). Environment texturing (`environmentTexturing = .automatic/.manual/.none`, `wantsHDREnvironmentTextures`) produces AREnvironmentProbeAnchor cube maps (`environmentTexture: (any MTLTexture)?`) for reflections; it is optional for a mapping app and costs GPU/thermal budget.
facts.availability: light estimation iOS 11.0+; environmentTexturing iOS 12.0+; wantsHDREnvironmentTextures iOS 13.0+
facts.notes: Note the enum is `ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.EnvironmentTexturing`, not `ARConfiguration.EnvironmentTexturing` (the latter path 404s). Leave environmentTexturing at .none for scanning to save power; consider ambientIntensity for exposure normalization of captured textures.

facts.claim: Plane detection can be combined with mesh reconstruction: `planeDetection = [.horizontal, .vertical]` yields ARPlaneAnchor objects (with `alignment`, `center`, `planeExtent` (iOS 16: width/height/rotationOnYAxis; `extent` is deprecated), `geometry: ARPlaneGeometry` (vertices/triangleIndices/boundaryVertices, convex hull), and `classification` (wall/floor/ceiling/table/seat/door/window/.none(status)); `ARPlaneAnchor.isClassificationSupported` is true on A12+). ARKit also uses detected planes to flatten the LiDAR mesh.
facts.availability: planeDetection iOS 11.0+; ARPlaneGeometry iOS 11.3+; classification iOS 12.0+; planeExtent/ARPlaneExtent iOS 16.0+
facts.notes: Plane anchor local frame: xz is the plane, +y is the normal; `center` is offset from anchor.transform (y always 0). Since iOS 16 the anchor transform is no longer rotated to fit the rectangle; apply `planeExtent.rotationOnYAxis` yourself. Plane anchors DO persist in ARWorldMap. Useful for the 2D floor plan (floor/wall/ceiling planes) alongside mesh classification.

facts.claim: Video format selection: `ARConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats` (class var, ordered highest quality first; default `videoFormat` = first entry) and `videoFormat` (instance). Each `ARConfiguration.VideoFormat` exposes `imageResolution` (landscape CGSize), `framesPerSecond`, `captureDevicePosition`, `captureDeviceType` (iOS 14.5), `isRecommendedForHighResolutionFrameCapturing` (iOS 16), `isVideoHDRSupported` (iOS 16), plus iOS 26-only `defaultPhotoSettings` and `defaultColorSpace`. 4K (3840x2160 @ 30) via `recommendedVideoFormatFor4KResolution` (class var, iOS 16, iPhone 11+/M1 iPad); HDR via `videoHDRAllowed` (iOS 16, non-binned/4K formats only).
facts.availability: videoFormat/supportedVideoFormats iOS 11.3+; captureDevicePosition iOS 13; captureDeviceType iOS 14.5; 4K/HDR/hi-res flags/configurableCaptureDevice iOS 16.0+; defaultPhotoSettings/defaultColorSpace iOS 26.0+
facts.notes: Typical iPhone 13 Pro formats (community): 1920x1440@60 (default, binned from 3840x2880), 1920x1080@60, 3840x2160@30 (4K). Changing videoFormat requires session.run(config) again. 4K and HDR increase power/thermal load and are discouraged for 60 fps experiences (WWDC22); for scanning keep 1920x1440@60 and use on-demand hi-res stills for textures. Do not reference `defaultPhotoSettings`/`defaultColorSpace` without `#available(iOS 26, *)`.

facts.claim: High-resolution still capture during a running session: `ARSession.captureHighResolutionFrame(completion:)` (iOS 16; async variant `captureHighResolutionFrame() async throws -> ARFrame`) returns an out-of-band ARFrame whose `capturedImage` is the full sensor photo (12 MP, 4032x3024 on iPhone 13 series) with full pose/anchors/intrinsics populated for that frame, without interrupting the 60 fps stream. For best results first set `config.videoFormat = ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.recommendedVideoFormatForHighResolutionFrameCapturing` (class var, may be nil on unsupported devices). Errors: `ARError.Code.highResolutionFrameCaptureInProgress` (only one in flight) and `.highResolutionFrameCaptureFailed`. iOS 26 adds `captureHighResolutionFrame(using: AVCapturePhotoSettings?, completion:)`.
facts.notes: 12 MP figure from WWDC22 'Discover ARKit 6' ('on iPhone 13 this means the full 12 megapixels of the Wide camera'); 4032x3024 reported by developers. Hi-res frame's capturedImage is the same YCbCr bi-planar format; camera.intrinsics/imageResolution on that frame describe the hi-res image. The hi-res frame does NOT carry sceneDepth (unsure: developers report depth is nil on the out-of-band frame; use the nearest regular frame's depth or the mesh). This is the intended path for texture photos and Object Capture photogrammetry input.

facts.claim: Raycasting against the LiDAR mesh: with sceneReconstruction enabled, `ARRaycastQuery.Target.estimatedPlane` with `TargetAlignment.any` intersects the scene mesh (including non-planar and featureless surfaces); with sceneReconstruction == [] raycasts ignore the mesh. `.existingPlaneGeometry` / `.existingPlaneInfinite` hit only ARPlaneAnchors. Apple's mesh sample uses `arView.raycast(from: tapLocation, allowing: .estimatedPlane, alignment: .any)`; the non-RealityKit path is `frame.raycastQuery(from:allowing:alignment:)` or `ARRaycastQuery(origin:direction:allowing:alignment:)` + `session.raycast(_:)` (results sorted nearest first) or `session.trackedRaycast(_:updateHandler:)`.
facts.availability: iOS 13.0+ (all raycast API); mesh intersection iOS 13.4+
facts.notes: `ARRaycastResult.anchor` is nil for estimatedPlane hits unless the ray also hits an existing plane, and the result gives no face index/normal beyond worldTransform orientation. For measurement-grade picking (edge snapping, face classification, normals) do your own CPU ray/triangle test (Moller-Trumbore) over your cached world-space mesh, as Apple's sample does a nearby-face search (5 cm) to fetch classification. `frame.hitTest(_:types:)` is deprecated; do not use. `ARFrame.raycastQuery(from:...)` builds the ray from a screen point using the frame's camera (viewport orientation handled internally; point is in the view's coordinate space when used via ARView, otherwise normalized image space? -> use ARView.raycast when you have an ARView, or build the ray yourself from unprojected screen points for a custom Metal view).

facts.claim: Session lifecycle: `run(_:options:)` transitions immediately (default options resume tracking and keep anchors); `pause()` stops tracking/capture. RunOptions: `.resetTracking`, `.removeExistingAnchors`, `.stopTrackedRaycasts`, `.resetSceneReconstruction` (clears the accumulated mesh). Running a configuration of a different class implicitly resets tracking; resetting tracking also removes existing anchors. Interruptions (backgrounding, camera taken by another app) arrive via `sessionWasInterrupted(_:)` / `sessionInterruptionEnded(_:)`; return true from `sessionShouldAttemptRelocalization(_:)` to let ARKit relocalize (state stays `.limited(.relocalizing)` until it recognizes the place), and call `run(config, options: [.resetTracking])` to give up. Errors via `session(_:didFailWithError:)` (ARError.Code e.g. `.cameraUnauthorized`, `.sensorUnavailable`, `.sensorFailed`, `.worldTrackingFailed`, `.unsupportedConfiguration`, `.invalidWorldMap`).
facts.availability: iOS 11.0+ (sessionShouldAttemptRelocalization, setWorldOrigin iOS 11.3+; identifier iOS 13.0+). Apple's JSON lists resetSceneReconstruction as iOS 11.0 but it is only meaningful with scene reconstruction (13.4+).
facts.notes: To change a setting (e.g. toggle planeDetection or videoFormat) mutate `session.configuration as? ARWorldTrackingConfiguration` (it is an @NSCopying copy) and call run again without reset options to keep tracking and anchors, exactly as Apple's mesh sample does. Use `.resetSceneReconstruction` when the user starts a new room in the same session, `[.resetTracking, .removeExistingAnchors]` when loading a world map. ARSessionDelegate/ARSessionObserver/ARSession are marked 'visionOS 1.0 deprecated' only on visionOS (irrelevant for iOS).

facts.claim: RoomPlan and your own ARKit mesh/depth pipeline can run on ONE ARSession: `RoomCaptureSession(arSession:)` (iOS 17) accepts your ARSession; RoomPlan 'honors any custom ARSession with ARWorldTrackingConfiguration' (WWDC23 10192), so your configuration (sceneReconstruction .meshWithClassification, frameSemantics sceneDepth, planeDetection, videoFormat) stays in effect while RoomPlan produces CapturedRoom data, and `stop(pauseARSession: false)` keeps the ARSession running between rooms so multi-room scans share one world coordinate frame (or save/restore ARWorldMap between sessions and wait for relocalization before `run(configuration:)`).
facts.api: class RoomCaptureSession { init(arSession: ARSession? = nil); var arSession: ARSession { get }; static var isSupported: Bool { get }; func run(configuration: RoomCaptureSession.Configuration); func stop(); func stop(pauseARSession: Bool); var delegate: (any RoomCaptureSessionDelegate)? }
facts.availability: RoomCaptureSession iOS 16.0+; init(arSession:) and stop(pauseARSession:) iOS 17.0+
facts.notes: This is the architectural hinge for 'raw LiDAR mesh + clean architectural model from the same walk-through'. Untested corner: whether RoomPlan itself re-runs the ARSession with its own configuration after `run(configuration:)` (the WWDC transcript says the custom session is honored; community reports from iOS 17 confirm mesh anchors keep arriving). Verify on device in the first build by logging `session.configuration` after RoomPlan starts. Details of RoomCaptureSession.Configuration, CapturedRoom and StructureBuilder belong to the roomplan topic.

facts.claim: Thermal and power: monitor `ProcessInfo.processInfo.thermalState` (`.nominal/.fair/.serious/.critical`) and `ProcessInfo.thermalStateDidChangeNotification` (must read `thermalState` once before subscribing). LiDAR + 60 fps camera + Metal is one of the heaviest workloads on an iPhone; throttling silently lowers GPU clocks and camera frame rate, which degrades world tracking and causes mesh drift. Also disable the idle timer during scans (`UIApplication.shared.isIdleTimerDisabled = true`).
facts.notes: Mitigations when state reaches .serious: drop smoothedSceneDepth, stop hi-res captures, lower render rate (MTKView.preferredFramesPerSecond), stop environment texturing, pause mesh post-processing; at .critical pause the session and tell the user. Also `ProcessInfo.processInfo.isLowPowerModeEnabled`.

facts.claim: Apple sample links and what they show: (1) 'Visualizing and interacting with a reconstructed scene' (iOS 13.4, RealityKit ARView): sets sceneReconstruction = .meshWithClassification with automaticallyConfigureSession = false, `arView.debugOptions.insert(.showSceneUnderstanding)` wireframe, toggles plane detection by mutating session.configuration and re-running, raycasts with `.estimatedPlane/.any`, walks `anchor.geometry.faces.count` on a background queue computing face centers in world space via `anchor.transform`, reads per-face classification, and enables `arView.environment.sceneUnderstanding.options.insert(.occlusion)` / `.physics`. (2) 'Displaying a point cloud using scene depth' (iOS 14, SwiftUI + Metal): frameSemantics [.sceneDepth, .smoothedSceneDepth], converts depthMap to .r32Float and confidenceMap to .r8Unorm Metal textures via CVMetalTextureCache, capturedImage Y/CbCr to .r8Unorm/.rg8Unorm, unprojects every depth pixel with scaled intrinsics in a vertex shader, filters by confidence, optionally upsamples depth 256x192 -> 960x760 with MPSImageGuidedFilter. (3) 'Creating a fog effect using scene depth' (iOS 15, Metal): smoothedSceneDepth, pixel-format switch for depth/confidence textures, MPSImageGaussianBlur.
facts.availability: samples require iOS 13.4 / 14.0 / 15.0; all build with Xcode 16
facts.notes: Point cloud sample: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/displaying-a-point-cloud-using-scene-depth ; fog sample: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/creating-a-fog-effect-using-scene-depth ; world map sample: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/saving-and-loading-world-data . A community mirror of the point-cloud sample source is github.com/seoyeong74/DisplayingAPointCloudUsingSceneDepth (ARDataProvider.swift, ARReceiver.swift, MetalPointCloud.swift, shaders.metal). The older WWDC20 'Visualizing a point cloud using scene depth' (accumulating cloud) page no longer resolves on developer.apple.com.

facts.claim: iOS 26 SDK ARKit diff versus iOS 18 SDK contains only additions relevant here (captureHighResolutionFrame(using:completion:), VideoFormat.defaultPhotoSettings, VideoFormat.defaultColorSpace) and the removal of ARQuickLookPreviewItem; no mesh, depth, raycast, world-map or session API used by this app was removed or deprecated at 26. The only deprecations in this area are the orientation-based ARCamera/ARFrame helpers (deprecated 27.0) and the long-deprecated hitTest/ARHitTestResult and ARPlaneAnchor.extent.
facts.notes: Verified from Apple doc JSON availability fields plus the .NET macios header diff for Xcode 26 b1. Nothing in this topic needs iOS 18 as a floor; the highest requirement is iOS 17 (RoomCaptureSession(arSession:)), iOS 16 for hi-res capture / planeExtent / exifData. iOS 18.0 deployment target is safe; iOS 17.0 would also work for everything listed.

facts.claim: ARFrame also exposes `rawFeaturePoints: ARPointCloud?` (`points: [simd_float3]`, `identifiers: [UInt64]`) - sparse visual features, unstable across frames, debugging only; `capturedDepthData` is TrueDepth (front camera) only and nil in world tracking; `segmentationBuffer` / `estimatedDepthData` exist only with person segmentation semantics.
facts.notes: Do not use rawFeaturePoints for geometry; use sceneDepth or the mesh.

gotchas: ARMeshAnchor geometry is anchor-local; forgetting `anchor.transform` puts every chunk at the origin (a very common bug, confirmed by Apple DTS). Compute world-space copies when you cache.

ARMeshGeometry buffers are reused/reallocated by ARKit on the next update for that anchor; SceneKit/RealityKit objects that wrap the MTLBuffer by reference crash or show garbage. Copy the bytes (memcpy from buffer.contents()) inside the delegate callback, respecting `offset` and `stride` (stride can be > 12).

`classification` is per FACE (count == faces.count) and one UInt8 per face; `normals` are per VERTEX despite the ARMeshGeometry doc prose saying 'each face includes a normal'. classification is nil with `.mesh` (no classification).

ARMeshClassification raw values: none=0, wall=1, floor=2, ceiling=3, table=4, seat=5, window=6, door=7. The doc topic lists cases alphabetically; do not derive raw values from that order. Use ARMeshClassification(rawValue:) rather than your own table.
ARWorldMap does not store ARMeshAnchors (DTS confirmed). Persist your own mesh; only planes and custom ARAnchors come back on relocalization.

Depth map is 256x192 landscape regardless of UI orientation, same FOV as capturedImage (1920x1440); scale intrinsics by (256/1920, 192/1440) before unprojecting, and read the real buffer size at runtime rather than hard-coding.

The ARCamera camera space looks down -z (+z toward the user); Apple's point-cloud shader uses z = +depth in a 'camera looks down +z' convention with its own projection, so when you convert depth pixels to ARKit world space use position = camera.transform * float4(x, -y, -depth, 1) with x,y from the pinhole formula (or equivalently flip both y and z). Verify with a known floor point on first device run.

On the iOS 26 SDK the orientation-based ARCamera helpers (`projectionMatrix(for:viewportSize:zNear:zFar:)`, `viewMatrix(for:)`, `displayTransform(for:viewportSize:)`) are the ones to call; the `viewRotationAngle:` replacements are iOS 27-only and would fail `#available` on iOS 18. Expect a deprecation warning at most.

`captureHighResolutionFrame` fails with `.highResolutionFrameCaptureInProgress` if a previous request is pending; serialize requests. `recommendedVideoFormatForHighResolutionFrameCapturing` can be nil (older devices); fall back to the default format (hi-res capture then still works but at lower still resolution). Depth on the hi-res frame should be treated as absent.

Changing `videoFormat`, `frameSemantics` or `sceneReconstruction` requires `session.run(config)` again; running with default options keeps tracking and anchors, but a format change can briefly stall frames.

`.estimatedPlane` raycasts return only worldTransform (position + surface-aligned orientation); no triangle index or classification. For measurement/snapping do a CPU ray-triangle test over your cached world-space mesh.

Mesh anchors can be removed and re-added seconds later (Apple forum report on iOS 18-era firmware); if you delete cached chunks on didRemove you lose data. Prefer marking chunks stale and re-adopting on didAdd with the same identifier.

ARFrame retention: holding ARFrames (e.g. queueing them for later texture extraction) starves the capture pipeline; ARKit logs a warning and tracking goes limited. Copy the pixel buffer (or convert to a texture/JPEG) immediately and drop the frame.
